Chapter 3: How Art Reflects Power, Property, and Status
Imagine stepping into the grand halls of an old museum. The walls are lined with oil paintings—portraits of wealthy merchants, noble families, and their sprawling estates. Those faces looking out at you? They’re framed by symbols of success: fine clothing, rare treasures, lush green landscapes. It’s like each painting quietly whispers a story about power and privilege.
Most of us might stroll past, admiring the beauty, maybe marveling at the artist’s skill and creativity. But if you look a little closer, there’s something deeper going on. These aren’t just pretty pictures—they’re stories about who gets to be seen, and why. Especially in Europe, the tradition of oil painting grew alongside the rise of private property. People who commissioned these works didn’t just want their faces painted. They wanted their possessions on display—their land, their jewels, their beloved animals. These paintings became visual inventories, recording wealth in vivid color.
Picture a merchant inviting an artist into his home, asking for a portrait of his family surrounded by the trappings of their success. Once finished, that artwork would hang in a place of honor, silently reminding every guest of the family’s status. Over time, these images became woven into society, quietly reinforcing the idea that a person’s worth could be measured by what they owned.
Here’s something to pay attention to: most people don’t realize how much this tradition still shapes the way we value art today. Oil painting, with its ability to capture the shine of silver, the softness of velvet, the sparkle of gemstones, was practically made for showing off material wealth. Every detail celebrates ownership—transforming possessions into symbols of identity.
But there’s even more to the story. The way people are posed in these paintings sends a message, too. Maybe there’s a landowner with one hand on a map, the other on a globe—showing off mastery over land and knowledge. Or a noblewoman seated among her treasures, her gaze calm and confident. The message? These are people who matter. Their lives are worth recording.
But what about everyone else? Servants, laborers, the poor—they show up only at the edges, if at all. They’re background characters, rarely the focus. It’s almost like each painting is a stage, and the drama of hierarchy plays out over and over again.
There’s a quiet discomfort that comes with this realization. The art filling our museums, the images we celebrate and preserve, often come from a world built on inequality. They reflect a time—and maybe even a present—where some lives are valued more than others, and property and status decide who’s important.
But with that discomfort comes a sense of possibility. What if we start looking more closely? What if we ask, “Who’s being seen—and who isn’t?” By questioning these old assumptions, we can see not just the beauty in a painting, but also the power it holds. And maybe, just maybe, we’ll start imagining new ways to see and understand the world around us.
